options: The increase in equity resulting from a business's ordinary, core operating activities
Cash received from any source, including loans
A type of liability owed to customers
The total amount of inventory a business has sold at cost
questions.explain: Revenue is the increase in equity that comes specifically from a business's core operations, like selling goods or services.

questions.q: A company performs $2,500 of consulting work for a client who will pay in 30 days. When is the revenue recorded?
options: Only once the cash is actually collected in 30 days
Today, when the work was substantially completed, even though cash has not been received
It is never recorded, since no cash changed hands immediately
Half now and half when paid
questions.explain: Revenue is recorded when earned — when the business has substantially done what it promised — not when cash is collected.

questions.q: A customer pays $12,000 upfront for a full year of subscription service. What happens to that $12,000 at the moment it's received?
options: All $12,000 is immediately recorded as revenue
None of it is recorded anywhere until the year is over
It is recorded as an expense
It is recorded mostly as a liability (Unearned Revenue), since the service has not yet been delivered
questions.explain: Cash received for services not yet performed is a liability (Unearned/Deferred Revenue) until it is actually earned.

questions.q: In the Palisade Creative Group example, what does the April 15 journal entry (collecting cash from the client) record?
options: An additional $9,000 of revenue
A decrease in revenue
No new revenue — just converting the Accounts Receivable asset into a Cash asset
A new liability
questions.explain: Collecting cash on an existing receivable creates zero new revenue; the revenue was already recorded when the work was completed.

questions.q: Why is 'revenue recognition' — deciding exactly when revenue has been earned — such a carefully governed area of accounting?
options: Because getting the timing wrong can misstate a business's financial results, and standards like ASC 606 exist to keep it consistent and auditable
Because it has no real impact on financial statements
Because revenue recognition only applies to government agencies
Because cash received and revenue earned are always identical, so there's nothing to govern
questions.explain: Revenue recognition timing has a major effect on reported financial results, which is why formal standards and systems like Oracle Fusion Receivables apply consistent, auditable rules.
